456.title: Two are better than one (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12)
456.hook: if one falls, the other lifts; a threefold cord is not quickly broken
456.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 is a common reading at Christian weddings, where the threefold cord is often explained as husband, wife and God; some couples braid three cords during the ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher's list of seasons. Your line: a time to speak.

Right before today's passage, the Preacher describes a man who has no one: no child, no brother. There's no end to his work, the text says, and his eyes are never satisfied with his money. He never stops to ask who all this is for. It's a sharp little portrait, and it could be someone you know: the one who answers emails at midnight, eats at the desk, and hasn't called a friend in a year. The Preacher has looked hard at everything under the sun and found most of it breath. But in the middle of all that hevel, he finds something that holds.
screen: `A MAN WITH NO ONE.` → `NO END TO HIS WORK.` → `WHO IS THIS FOR?` → `SOMETHING THAT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour." Then the Preacher gives three pictures, all very physical. First, the fall: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." A road at night, a ditch, a twisted ankle. Second, the cold: two lying together keep each other warm, but how can one be warm alone? Third, the attack: someone might overpower a person alone, but two can stand against him. Fall, cold, danger. Each time, a second person is the difference. Then, almost as a proverb tacked on the end, the line your carry comes from: "and a threefold cord is not quickly broken." Twist two strands together and they're stronger. Twist in a third and the rope holds far more. The Preacher counted two, and then the proverb says three. Readers have wondered about that. At Christian weddings, the third strand is often heard as God, woven in with the couple. Others hear it simply as a proverb about community: two is good, more is better. The text itself doesn't say who the third strand is. But here's the striking thing: the Preacher who called everything breath doesn't call friendship breath. In a book that doubts almost everything, he's sure of this.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who once lifted you when you fell, a hard week, a bad diagnosis, a breakup, a day you couldn't get off the couch, and remember one specific thing they did: the call, the meal, the ride, the hour they just sat there. Notice how that time might have gone alone, and find the plain words you'd use to thank them. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Hevel. The Preacher's word for breath or vanity, used throughout Ecclesiastes for what doesn't last, except, he says, for a friend who helps you up.
Your line: a threefold cord. Two strands hold, and a third holds more. Day four hundred fifty-six.

457.title: Remember now your creator (Ecclesiastes 12:1–8)
457.hook: before the silver cord is loosed
457.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 12 is read at some Christian funerals, especially for older people, and its opening verse is often taught to young people in churches and youth groups as a call not to put faith off until later.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amid all that hevel, something that holds. Your line: a threefold cord.

A big old house, at the end of a day. The guards at the door tremble. The strong men are stooped. The women who grind the grain have stopped, because too few are left. Those who look out of the windows find everything dim. The doors to the street are shut, and the sound of the mill is low. Someone wakes at the first chirp of a bird. The almond tree is in bloom, all white. It sounds like a ghost story. It's a riddle. He's describing a body growing old.
screen: `A HOUSE AT THE END OF THE DAY.` → `THE GRINDERS CEASE.` → `IT'S A RIDDLE.` → `A BODY GROWING OLD.`

segments.voice: The poem opens, in the King James Bible: "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them." One old way of reading decodes the riddle of the house. The keepers of the house who tremble are the hands and arms. The strong men bowing are the legs and back. The grinders that cease because they are few are the teeth. Those who look out of the windows are the eyes. Waking at the sound of a bird is light sleep in old age. And the almond tree in white blossom is white hair. Not every reader takes each image the same way, and some hear a whole town falling into ruin as well as a body. Then the images turn to endings: "Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken." A lamp on a silver chain: the chain snaps, the golden bowl of oil shatters, the light goes out. A pitcher breaks at the well. And then: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." Now back to the first word, remember. In Hebrew it's not only recalling a fact. It means keeping someone in mind and acting on it, the way God remembers Noah in the flood and sends the wind. So remember your Creator isn't nostalgia. It's: live toward God now, while your hands are steady and your eyes are clear. The Preacher isn't trying to frighten the young. He's urging them not to wait.

segments.voice: Feel your hands open and close slowly; notice your eyes taking in light, your ears catching small sounds. Whatever your age, your body can do things now that it may not always do. If you pray, offer today's strength back to the One who gave it; if not, hold the thought that this strength is here now, and not forever.

Your line: remember, while you're young. You're younger today than you'll ever be again. Day four hundred fifty-seven, done.

458.title: Love as strong as death (Song of Songs 8:6–7)
458.hook: many waters cannot quench love; a book of love poetry in the Bible
458.howItsDone: Song of Songs 8:6–7 is a frequent reading at Christian weddings; the book has a long history of devotional reading as a picture of God's love, and in Jewish practice it is read at Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher's last poem, the silver cord and the golden bowl. Your line: remember, while you're young.

Some people open the Bible expecting rules and are startled to find this. A woman searching the city streets at night for the one she loves. A man comparing her hair to a flock of goats coming down a mountainside, which was a compliment. Gardens, spices, vineyards, doves, a knock at the door. Two voices, longing for each other, out loud. A whole book of love poetry, right after Ecclesiastes. And near its end, the woman says something so strong it's still read at weddings.
screen: `SEARCHING THE CITY AT NIGHT.` → `HAIR LIKE A FLOCK OF GOATS.` → `A WHOLE BOOK OF LOVE POETRY.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death." A seal in the ancient world was a stamp carved in stone, worn on a cord around the neck or on a ring. It was your signature, your identity. Set me as a seal on your heart means: carry me, let me be the mark you press into everything. And love is as strong as death. Not stronger. As strong. Death is the one thing nothing escapes, and love, she says, holds on just as hard. Then: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." In the Bible, the great waters are chaos, the flood, the sea that swallows. Love isn't put out by them. And if a man offered everything he owned for love, he'd be laughed at. Love can't be bought. Now a surprise: God is barely named in this book, if at all. Some read one word in verse six, describing love's flame, as containing a short form of God's name; many others read it simply as a mighty flame. So why is it in the Bible? Readers answer more than one way. Jewish tradition has long read it as the love between God and Israel; a famous rabbi called it the holy of holies among the writings. Christian readers from the early church on have read it as the love between Christ and the church, or God and the soul. And readers also honor it as human love, desire and faithfulness, celebrated as good.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, a partner, a parent, a child, a friend of many years, and think of the floods it has come through: a move, an argument, an illness, a loss. 459.title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
459.hook: in a book of ruins: his mercies are new every morning
459.howItsDone: Many Christians sing the hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness, drawn from Lamentations 3:22–23, and some read the verses at the start of the day; in Jewish practice the whole book of Lamentations is chanted on Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Songs and a seal on the heart, and your line: many waters cannot quench love. Today, a poem written in the ruins.

Jerusalem has fallen. The Babylonian army has broken through the walls, burned the Temple, and marched much of the city's population away. Streets that were full are empty. Children faint from hunger at the corners. The roads to the city mourn, the text says, because no one comes to the feasts anymore. Someone sat in that ruin and wrote five poems about it: the book of Lamentations. Raw grief, long stretches of pain, no tidy answers. And right in the middle of the middle poem, a line hopeful enough to end up in a hymn.
screen: `JERUSALEM HAS FALLEN.` → `FIVE POEMS OF GRIEF.` → `A LINE OF HOPE IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Just before it, the poet is at the bottom. He's been walled in, his prayers shut out; he's forgotten what happiness is. Then he calls something to mind, and hope rises. In the King James Bible: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Notice what he doesn't say. The city isn't rebuilt. The grief isn't over; it goes on for two more chapters. One thing hasn't run out: God's mercies. The Hebrew word is chesed, steadfast loving-kindness. New every morning: not stored up from yesterday, not a fixed supply that gets used up, but delivered fresh, like the manna in the desert that had to be gathered each day. The book's shape holds a detail too. Four of the five poems are acrostics, each verse or stanza starting with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The third poem, where this line sits, triples it: three verses for every letter, sixty-six in all. Grief put in order, letter by letter, as if to say: we will grieve this completely. And at the center of it, this. The author isn't named in the text; an old tradition credits the prophet Jeremiah. Jewish communities read Lamentations each year on Tisha B'Av, mourning the Temple's fall. And a Methodist writer named Thomas Chisholm later drew on this line for the hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness.

segments.voice: Think of the ruin in your own week, a mistake you made, a hurt you carried, a thing that didn't get fixed, and don't pretend it isn't there; the poet didn't. Then picture tomorrow morning, light coming in, the first breath of the day, and imagine waking without dragging today's weight into it, not because it's solved, but because the morning is new. If you pray, you can say the line itself: great is thy faithfulness.
Chesed. Hebrew for steadfast loving-kindness, the mercy Lamentations says doesn't run out in a ruined city, but comes fresh each day, new every morning.
Your line: great is thy faithfulness. Even in the ruins, the mercies come fresh. Day four hundred fifty-nine, done.

460.title: The books between (Wisdom 3:1–3)
460.hook: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Wisdom, Sirach and others; Protestants often call them Apocrypha
460.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians read the deuterocanonical books in worship, and Wisdom 3:1–9 is a common reading at Catholic funerals; Anglican and Episcopal churches read from the Apocrypha in their lectionaries, while many other Protestant churches read them privately, if at all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a line of hope in a book of ruins, mercies new every morning, and your line: great is thy faithfulness.

Put three Bibles side by side on a table: one from a Catholic parish, one from a Greek Orthodox church, one from a Baptist church down the street. They all begin with Genesis and end with Revelation. But count the books, and the counts don't match. The Protestant Bible has sixty-six. The Catholic Bible has seventy-three. Orthodox Bibles have a few more again. Same faith in Christ, same Gospels, different shelves. It comes down to a handful of books from the centuries just before Jesus, and what each church calls them.
screen: `THREE BIBLES ON A TABLE.` → `SIXTY-SIX, SEVENTY-THREE, AND MORE.` → `WHY DON'T THE COUNTS MATCH?`

segments.voice: They include Tobit, Judith, the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, and First and Second Maccabees, plus extra passages in Esther and Daniel. Most were written, or survive, in Greek, in the Greek Old Testament many early Christians read. Catholics call them deuterocanonical: deutero means second, canon means the measuring rule, the list. Second-listed, not second-rate: their place on the list was settled later, after some debate. The Council of Trent confirmed them for Catholics in 1546. Orthodox churches also read them, and include a few others. In the Reformation, Martin Luther gathered these books into their own section between the testaments: not equal to scripture, he said, but useful and good to read. Many Protestants call them the Apocrypha, from a Greek word for hidden. The 1611 King James Bible itself printed them between the testaments, and Anglicans still read from them in worship. So: Catholics and Orthodox Christians hold them as scripture. Many Protestants honor them as edifying history and wisdom, but not as scripture. Now a taste of one. The Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek, speaks of good people who die young or unjustly. In the King James Apocrypha: "But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and there shall no torment touch them." To the foolish, it goes on, they seemed to die, but they are in peace. It's read at funerals across traditions: whatever shelf you keep it on, people have held this line at gravesides for a very long time.

segments.voice: Let the line come back slowly, word by word: the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God. Then bring to mind someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to, and picture them held, not lost. If you pray, you can entrust them to God with the line itself; if you don't, just sit with them a moment in that picture of an open hand.
Deuterocanon. The second-listed books, like Wisdom and Sirach: scripture for Catholics and the Orthodox, the Apocrypha for many Protestants.
Your line: in the hand of god. Held there, not lost, at every graveside. See you tomorrow.

461.title: Block close: the prayer book
461.hook: psalms for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good
461.howItsDone: Christians pray the Psalms daily in many forms: monastic communities and the Liturgy of the Hours cycle through them, Orthodox services read the whole Psalter each week, Anglicans pray them through each month, and many Protestants read one a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the deuterocanon, and a line held at gravesides: in the hand of god.

Fifty days ago this part of the Bible opened with a tree planted by the water. Since then: a psalm for the night sky and a psalm for the dark night. My God, my God, why. A clean heart, asked for after a terrible failure. Help from the hills. Out of the depths. By the rivers of Babylon. Then Job, a good man who lost everything, and his friends, wise for seven days, until they started talking. Then Proverbs, the Preacher, the Song and Lamentations. So what was all of it?
screen: `FIFTY DAYS SINCE THE TREE.` → `PSALMS, JOB, PROVERBS.` → `THE PREACHER AND THE SONG.` → `WHAT WAS ALL OF IT?`

segments.voice: Start with the Psalms. For many centuries they've been the prayer book of Jews and of Christians: monks chant all hundred and fifty in a cycle, churches sing them on Sunday, people whisper them in hospital beds. And the surprise is how much of it isn't polite. There's joy, in the King James words: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." There's trust: the Lord is my shepherd. But there's also rage, confusion, how long, O Lord, and one psalm, the eighty-eighth, that ends in darkness with no answer at all. A large share of the psalms are laments. This prayer book teaches you to bring the real feeling, not the tidy one. The early church writer Athanasius wrote that in the rest of scripture we read about others, but in the Psalms we find our own words, as if they were written for us. The wisdom books keep the same honesty. Job won't accept a cheap answer for suffering, and in the end God says Job spoke rightly and his explainers did not. Proverbs puts wisdom in ordinary life: the tongue, the work, the ant. The Preacher says life is breath, so eat your bread with joy. The Song says love is as strong as death. Lamentations finds mercies new every morning, even in the ruins. Put together, one idea these books share is that everything a human being feels can be brought before God. The Gospels show Jesus praying a psalm on the cross. Read like this, the prayer book isn't there to make anyone sound holy; it's there to make them honest.

462.title: What a prophet is
462.hook: one who speaks for God, usually uncomfortably, to their own people
462.howItsDone: Christians read the prophets throughout the church year, especially in Advent and Lent, and many churches see the prophets' call for justice as part of their own work with the poor; Jewish communities read a passage from the Prophets, the haftarah, every Sabbath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block close on the prayer book, and your line: pray what you feel.

A king has done something terrible. He took another man's wife, and when she became pregnant, he arranged for her husband to die in battle. Nobody at court will say a word. Then a man named Nathan comes and tells the king a story: a rich man with huge flocks steals a poor man's only lamb, a lamb the poor man's children loved, to serve to a guest. The king is furious. That man deserves to die, he says. And Nathan looks at King David and says four words, in the King James Bible: "Thou art the man." A new block, and a question: what is a prophet?
screen: `A KING'S COVER-UP.` → `A STORY ABOUT A STOLEN LAMB.` → `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: In everyday speech, a prophet predicts the future; in the Bible, that's a small part. The Greek prophetes means one who speaks for, or speaks forth: a spokesperson. The Hebrew is navi, and some scholars think it means one who is called, or one who calls out. Either way, the job is less fortune-telling than forth-telling: saying what God sees, now, out loud. And they spoke mostly to their own people: kings, priests and neighbors, about their own injustice: the poor cheated in the market, widows ignored, worship that was all show. It was rarely welcome. Jeremiah was beaten and thrown in a pit. Amos was told to go home. Some weren't professionals at all: Amos said he was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but a herdsman and a tender of fig trees. And they weren't only stern. The same voices that warned also comforted: Isaiah, tomorrow's prophet, speaks of swords beaten into plowshares, and of a God who will not forget his people even if a mother could forget her child. In Christian Bibles, the prophets close the Old Testament: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel, called the major prophets because their books are long, with Lamentations beside Jeremiah, then twelve shorter ones. Jewish Bibles arrange them differently, and count books like Joshua and Kings among the prophets too. In Matthew's Gospel the crowds call Jesus a prophet, and he says, "A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house." Christians honor him as more than a prophet, and also see him standing in this line.
screen: `NOT FORETELLING: FORTH-TELLING.` · `TO THEIR OWN PEOPLE.` · `A HERDSMAN, NOT A PROFESSIONAL.` · `MAJOR MEANS LONG, NOT IMPORTANT.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Think of something someone told you recently that stung, a criticism from a friend, a hard word from a boss, and notice the defense forming. Set it aside a moment and ask honestly: is there any truth in it, not all of it, just any? Hold that piece without arguing, and if you pray, ask for ears to hear it.
Prophet. Navi in Hebrew, prophetes in Greek: one called to speak for God, usually uncomfortably, and usually to their own people.
Your line: truth to power. Said out loud, and rarely welcome. Day four hundred sixty-two.
